results.title: Nebius, Oracle, and Vessl AI Push AI Rental Rates Higher as Delivery Tightens | Drip
highlights:
# Nebius, Oracle, and Vessl AI Push AI Rental Rates Higher as Delivery Tightens

AI rental prices are climbing as cloud providers monetize the growing cost and scarcity of delivering usable GPU capacity.

Updated September 28, 2026

## What is this trend?

GPU rental rates are rising as cloud and AI operators pass through higher costs for power, cooling, and delivery constraints on already-contracted capacity.

- • Nebius, Oracle, and Vessl AI are raising prices on specific GPU offerings, not the whole market.
- • Scarcity is shifting from chips alone to deliverable capacity: power, cooling, and site readiness.
- • Utility delays and high-density racks are making retrofits and interconnects a billable constraint.
- • Operators with power and thermal control can command higher rents and better margins.
- • Pricing is fragmenting by region and SKU as guaranteed access becomes more valuable than headline supply.

## What’s the latest?

September 28, 2026

Nebius raised selected Nvidia GPU rates 17%–21%, Oracle renewed expiring GPU contracts about 20% higher, and Vessl AI lifted H100 pricing in Korea by 24.7%, where local H100 rentals were up 21.9% month over month to $3.2

results.title: NVIDIA GPU price rise pushes up AI infrastructure costs
highlights:
AI News September 01, 2026 01:01 AM 

 

NVIDIA’s soaring GPU prices and continued memory shortages are increasing AI infrastructure costs worldwide, forcing cloud providers and enterprises to rethink how they secure affordable computing capacity.

For businesses and startups using artificial intelligence, the impact could eventually be higher costs to run AI systems. As companies already struggle with the growing computing costs of processing large volumes of AI tokens, expensive hardware could add further pressure.

NVIDIA’s RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU is now listed at $16,000 on its US Marketplace, compared with $13,250 earlier this year and about $8,565 when it launched in March 2025. The rise in the cost of powerful AI hardware comes as the world faces a shortage of memory chips, another key component needed to run AI systems and data centres.

The problem is being driven by the rapid expansion of AI. Technology companies are building more data centres and buying large quantities of GPUs and memory chips to train and run AI models. This has increased demand faster than suppliers can expand production.

Research firm TrendForce expects memory supplies to remain tight through 2027. It has said companies making memory chips are increasingly focusing their production on specialised memory used in AI systems and servers, leaving less supply available for other customers.

The shortage matters because memory chips are needed alongside powerful processors. When the cost of these components rises, cloud providers and companies running AI infrastructure face higher costs.

Large technology companies are in a stronger position because they can buy equipment and secure supplies through long-term agreements. Smaller cloud providers, startups and businesses may have less bargaining power and could end up paying more.

The pressure is also reaching India.

“NVIDIA's pricing is driven largely by demand and component costs, especially memory, which remains tight and is projected to rise through 2027. Blended across our existing fleet and volume purchase commitments, we anticipate GPU cloud pricing in India to rise by 15–20% over the next 12–18 months, unless memory supply eases or alternative architectures gain traction,” said Ishan Talathi, Founder & CEO, CloudPe.

...

For companies using AI, the rising cost is also changing the decision between buying expensive hardware and renting computing power from cloud providers.

Buying GPUs can make sense for companies that use them constantly, but it requires a large upfront investment and brings electricity, maintenance and upgrade costs. Renting avoids those expenses but leaves companies exposed to changes in cloud prices.

results.title: CFTC Moves to Make AI Compute a Regulated, Tradable Commodity | AI2Work
highlights:
## Key Takeaways

- 1 The CFTC's August 19 request for comment is a fact-finding step, not a rule. It creates no new obligations, but it signals that the agency intends to build a regulatory pathway for compute derivatives, with comments closing October 20, 2026.
- 2 The RFC cites academic estimates placing the annual gross compute service flow at roughly $430 billion to $1.3 trillion, or about 1.4% to 4.0% of U.S. GDP, while noting that most pricing still happens in undisclosed bilateral deals.
- 3 Three venues have already announced compute futures ahead of any final framework. CME Group and Silicon Data are targeting October 5, 2026, subject to regulatory review, which puts the exchanges roughly two weeks ahead of the comment file closing.

For most of the AI buildout, the price of compute has been a private number. Two companies renting identical Nvidia H100 capacity in the same month could pay rates that differ by a factor of two, and neither had a public benchmark to check the other against. That opacity is now a federal policy question.

On August 19, 2026, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission issued a Request for Comment on the Listing of Compute Derivatives Contracts, published in the Federal Register two days later at 91 FR 54259. Chairman Michael S. Selig framed it as the first step toward rules of the road for American compute markets, invoking the way U.S. exchanges came to set global benchmarks for the commodities that powered the industrial economy.

The timing is unusually tight. The comment file closes October 20, 2026. CME Group and Silicon Data have already announced plans to list two cash-settled compute futures contracts on October 5, subject to regulatory review, which means the market may begin trading before the consultation that is meant to inform its oversight has even closed.

## The Numbers Behind the Filing

The CFTC's own framing of the compute market, alongside current benchmark pricing, sets the scale of what is being regulated.

$430B–$1.3T

Estimated annual gross compute service flow

Academic estimates cited in CFTC Request for Comment, August 2026

$2.53 H100 neo-cloud rental, USD per GPU-hour Silicon Data H100 Rental Price Index (ticker SDH100RT)

Oct 20, 2026 Deadline for public comment Federal Register, 91 FR 54259

...

The RFC is a fact-finding instrument, not a proposed rule. It creates no obligations and imposes no requirements. What it does is put a structured set of questions to the market about whether compute can satisfy the statutory Core Principles that govern designated contract markets, or DCMs, under the Commodity Exchange Act.

...

Three venues have announced compute futures products, all pending regulatory review. Whichever contract attracts liquidity first is likely to become the reference price for the sector, in the same way ICE Brent and CME WTI came to anchor crude oil. Note that none of these contracts had received final approval as of the most recent public reporting.

| Venue | Index partner | Contracts announced | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CME Group (listed on NYMEX) | Silicon Data, backed by DRW | H100 Rental Index Futures and B200 Rental Index Futures, each representing a month of hourly rental cost | Launch targeted October 5, 2026, pending regulatory review |
| Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) | Ornn, publisher of the Ornn Compute Price Index | Cash-settled, USD-denominated GPU futures referencing H100, H200, B200 and RTX 5090 series | Announced May 19, 2026, pending regulatory approval |
| Architect Financial Technologies (AX exchange) | Ornn | Futures tied to GPU and DRAM prices | Announced January 2026, with a US exchange plan disclosed in May 2026 |

...

The most striking thing about the RFC is that the Commission argues against its own premise as forcefully as it argues for it. The document states that compute may not yet exhibit several characteristics that normally underpin a commodity derivatives market, specifically fungibility, standardization, and sufficient liquidity. It describes price formation as fragmented and largely occurring in opaque bilateral transactions, and it warns that dominant participants may hold enough pricing power to make a settlement index manipulable.

...

What is not in dispute is the volatility. Silicon Data's published index history shows H100 rental prices falling roughly 45% from index inception into February 2025 before recovering, and B200 dropping about 20% from a September peak before rallying more than 40% off the low. Providers and renters on the wrong side of those moves absorbed the full swing with no instrument to offset it.

...

- Quantify your actual exposure: annual GPU-hours contracted, the share on spot versus reserved terms, and how much of your gross margin moves with a 20% swing in rental rates.
- Check whether the proposed settlement indices track the hardware, region, and contract structure you actually buy — an H100 neo-cloud benchmark is a poor hedge for reserved B200 capacity in a different geography.
- Model the basis risk explicitly. A cash-settled index hedge offsets index movement, not your negotiated bilateral price, and the residual gap is the number your CFO will ask about.
- Review existing compute supply agreements for clauses that may be affected by a regulated forward curve, including price-adjustment and benchmark-reference language.
- Decide whether to file a comment before October 20, 2026, directly or through an industry association — the Commission asked for empirical data, and firms with real transaction records have disproportionate influence on the record.
- If you sell compute capacity, assess whether your pricing disclosures could be read as contributing to a settlement index, and what surveillance or information-sharing obligations might follow.
- Track whether the CME and ICE contracts receive final approval and how open interest develops in the first quarter of trading, since a thin market is a worse hedge than no hedge at all.

results.title: CME wants to list GPU rental futures on October 5
highlights:
# CME wants to list GPU rental futures on October 5

Two contracts, one month of rental each, cash settled against a rental index.

Nejla Ayvazoglu

## THE TEARDOWN

You cannot store an hour of GPU time. That single fact is why this contract is hard to build.

### The Structural Signal

CME Group and Silicon Data announced two compute futures on August 11, 2026. Trading is targeted for October 5, pending CFTC review.

Both are cash settled and listed under NYMEX rules. One tracks the Silicon Data H100 rental index, the other the B200 index.

Each contract stands for roughly one month of GPU rental. The underlying is an hourly rental rate for a specific Nvidia chip.

The CFTC moved in the same week. It sent a draft request for public comment on compute derivatives to the White House budget office in mid-August.

Bloomberg reported it on August 17. The request is pre-rule, and no comment deadline had been published as of late August.

Chairman Michael Selig framed the stakes bluntly. "America cannot win the AI race without a robust derivatives market for compute," he said.

...

### The Mechanical Breakdown

Start with what makes this hard. 

An unsold hour expires. That kills the cost-of-carry link that anchors the curve in oil, metals, and grain.

Without carry, the forward price is pure expectation. No warehouse arbitrage keeps it honest.

Now the index. Silicon Data collects hourly on-demand rental prices for H100 and B200 chips across providers.

Those prices are not comparable out of the box. Region, network speed, storage, contract length, and uptime all change what an hour is worth.

So the index normalizes them. That normalization is the product, and everything else is packaging.

ICE went further down the same road. Its index measures tokenized compute and connectivity after adjusting capacity for energy use.

Read that carefully. Two rival benchmarks now define one unit of compute in two different ways.

Settlement is the last step. The contract pays against the index average, with no chips delivered anywhere.

Clearing sits at CME. Margin, daily marks, and a clearing house standing between the two sides.

...

The index tracks on-demand spot rates. Those two numbers can drift apart for months.

Liquidity is the second risk. The natural sellers are data centers, and the biggest buyers own their own chips.

Hyperscalers do not need this hedge. That thins the pool to mid-size labs, resellers, and speculators.

Concentration is the third. If a handful of providers set most of the input prices, the benchmark is easy to lean on.

results.title: AI淘金潮下，算力租赁到底有多赚钱？ | 投中网
highlights:
AI Agent、大模型越往商业化走，算力就越像一张越来越紧俏的“船票”。 

训练模型、上线推理服务、承接企业客户，看起来比拼的是模型能力，背后却都绕不开同一个问题：有没有充足、稳定且价格合适的算力。高端GPU难买，机房、电力、网络和运维资源同样紧张，自建集群成本高、周期长，许多公司只能转向租赁。

于是，算力租赁变成了AI产业链上最热闹的一门生意之一。除了公有云服务商、电信运营商、专业算力租赁商、第三方IDC，一些中小创业团队也参与到了算力淘金潮中，有人靠芯片货源赚钱，有人靠机房和跨境渠道赚钱，也有人把算力与模型、运维、合规服务打包出售。

...

算力租赁不是一个新生意，但AI大模型的爆发彻底改变了行业的供需天平。

中国信通院数据显示，2026年一季度国内算力租赁市场规模达680亿元，同比增长62%，预计全年将突破2600亿元。其中，国内AI算力需求同比大增417%，而供给增速仅128%。

在国内的市场环境中，高端GPU供给持续受限，下游需求持续膨胀，卖方市场成为所有从业者最直观的感受。虽然算力租赁市场里，大玩家牢牢占据大部分市场份额，但也有不少创业者在缝隙中寻找机会。

先有客户场景，再补充算力供给的“需求驱动”是常见的入局方式。

...

产业研究者维克夏的调研显示，海外不少企业对外出租算力，是盘活自用业务溢出的闲置资源，硬件折旧大多已经由内部业务消化；而国内多数算力租赁主体，硬件采购、机房建设依托租赁业务回款来覆盖，经营杠杆压力更高。

入场路径不同，计价方式和回本逻辑自然不同。

王岩的科研算力业务有着行业通用的标准计费逻辑：CPU超算按“核时”计费，即一颗CPU核心运行一小时，价格区间在0.04元到0.1元每核时；GPU按“卡时”计费，4090显卡约2到4元每卡时，5090显卡约3.5到5元每卡时。定价是按照3到5年的硬件回本周期倒推，他所在的公司内部以4年回本作为测算标准，硬件涨价则租赁价格同步上调。

ian的跨境算力生意则采用双轨计价。面向国内客户的H200服务器，单台月租金最高可达10.5万元人民币；面向海外客户的GB200，则按550到830美元每小时的标准报价。PRO6000这类中端卡，卡时租金约1.5到2美元。

在他的实操经验里，主流型号服务器的正常回本周期在2.5到3年，这是行业公认的经营底线。

前述商务负责人则提到，行业内普遍的回本周期在12到18个月，这一数据差异源于业务结构的不同：聚焦Token售卖、高利用率的高端算力，回本速度更快；而分散、低负载的通用算力，回本周期则明显拉长。

利润空间同样分化明显。

王岩所在的科研赛道，CPU超算业务利润率约30%，GPU智算业务利润率仅5%到10%，核心原因是高端GPU采购成本暴涨，但终端租赁价格涨幅跟不上硬件溢价，中间商利润被大幅挤压。能够拿到一手货源的ian在市场中则如鱼得水。

不过所有人都认同一件事：这是绝对的卖方市场。

英伟达高端GPU拿不到货，高端训练卡普遍要签1到3年长约，客户排着队等算力释放。手里有卡的，掌握定价权；硬件涨价，租赁报价跟着涨。即便出现空置，新需求也很快填上。所以服务商挑客户也挑得理直气壮：与其追短期高价散单，不如锁定长期稳定租约，现金流好看，融资也好谈。

...

王岩直言，整条产业链里，资方是最赚钱的环节，手握大额资金，出资采购服务器硬件，和客户签署3到5年的长租协议，违约成本极高，收益确定性极强。2024到2025年低价采购的一批高端算力，原本测算3到5年回本，随着硬件价格暴涨，回本周期直接压缩到两年左右，既赚租金收益，又赚资产增值的红利。相比之下，机房服务商、网络带宽提供商、直面客户的销售服务商，只能分到很小一部分利润。

...

首先是需求结构的根本性切换：算力需求正从纯训练主导向“训练+推理”并重迁移，推理算力增速已超纯训练。

王岩认为，推理业务对中小型服务商更加友好，推理场景对显卡型号要求灵活，4090、5090这类消费级显卡就能支撑，资源匹配难度低，不容易受到高端卡进出口管制的直接冲击。

前述商务负责人也提到，客户越来越看重Token成本与低延迟，单纯的硬件时长租赁已经无法匹配需求，行业正在从卖硬件时长向卖算力产出过渡。

...

算力租赁会一直是个好生意吗？

在王岩看来，2027年行业或将迎来新一轮算力荒，高端可流通算力进一步收缩，硬件与算力租赁近1年还会持续上涨，高昂的成本会倒逼大模型行业降温，一部分资金储备薄弱的初创企业会退出市场。等到价格上涨到临界点，市场经历一轮洗牌后，硬件与租赁价格最终会回归合理区间。

ian则认为，短期3到5年内，高端芯片的稀缺性不会根本改变，行业核心矛盾始终是稳定获取货源。

results.title: You are negotiating the wrong term for your AI contract — Aureak
highlights:
In September 2026 an identical H100 rented for anywhere between $1.49 and $10.98 an hour, and spot prices were up a third on the year for a three-year-old chip. No rate you negotiate survives that, while the terms that decide the outcome are signed without much negotiation.

...

The reason to write it up now is that the market has changed underneath the contracts being signed against it. For three years, AI compute procurement was a scarcity problem: you took what you could get, on the terms offered, and the only real question was whether you got an allocation at all. The supply position has since become far harder to read, and the negotiating posture most buyers learned during the shortage is now costing them money.

Duration compounds it. Agreements signed this year run three to five years, spanning roughly two and a half accelerator generations and a meaningful shift in how much of the world’s AI capacity is available on an open market at all — by which I mean a market where any buyer can purchase from several sellers at a price they can discover. Almost none of that risk is addressed by the rate.

...

Start with a fact that ought to be impossible in a functioning market. In September 2026, renting one H100 for one hour cost between $1.49 and $10.98 depending on where you bought it — Vast.ai’s peer-to-peer floor at the bottom, Google Cloud’s a3-highgpu-8g list price at the top, for the same silicon. 1 Cross-provider medians land in between and disagree with each other: AIMultiple tracked $3.38 in August 2026, the Mercatus index $3.84 across 27 providers in September. 2 

Now the direction. The expected pattern for a three-year-old chip is steady decline as newer silicon takes the premium workloads. That is not what happened. Bank of America put H100 spot at $2.77–$2.80 an hour in August 2026 — up 2% on the month and up 33% on the year. A100 pricing, on a chip two generations old, was up 17% year on year. 2 

Anyone who signed a multi-year fixed-rate commitment in 2024, when H100 rentals were above $7 an hour, is now paying well above the market median. Anyone who deliberately stayed on spot through 2026 expecting further declines paid a third more than they budgeted. Both bets were reasonable when made, and both are wrong in hindsight.

The reason is that the binding constraint moved, and it did not move to where anyone was looking. It is no longer GPU die output. Morgan Stanley described DRAM as having become the principal bottleneck in the AI buildout, with memory prices up roughly six-fold over the prior year as manufacturers redirected HBM and DRAM toward data-center parts. 3 Nvidia has been unusually plain about the consequence: CFO Colette Kress told analysts in November 2025 that “the clouds are sold out,” and by August 2026 Jensen Huang was telling investors the company had “supply for 70% growth, but demand is much higher.” Kress added that supply would remain a bottleneck at least through the end of fiscal 2028. 2 

The same tightness shows up in captive silicon, and the buyers are saying so on the record. In April 2026 Anthropic committed more than $100bn to AWS over ten years and secured up to 5 GW of capacity spanning Trainium2 through Trainium4, with an option on later generations. Andy Jassy’s stated reason: the silicon is “in such hot demand.” 4 Hyperscaler list prices, meanwhile, move slowest of all, because they are set through multi-year commercial agreements rather than marketplace clearing: AWS cut P5 pricing 44% in June 2025, and the resulting $6.88 an hour is still roughly 2.7 times a marketplace rate. 5 

So the honest summary is not “prices fell.” It is that the same chip traded across a seven-fold range in a single month, moved in opposite directions depending on which tier you bought, and did so because of a constraint — memory — that was not the one the market had been watching. You cannot win this negotiation on price. What you can do is decide in advance what happens when the price you agreed turns out to be wrong. That is a question about terms.

...

The unit of commitment. The highest-leverage term in the document, routinely treated as a drafting detail. A commitment in dollars is worth far more than one in GPU-hours, which beats one tied to a named configuration. Some providers offer portfolio draw-down — the right to spend across the vendor’s range rather than one SKU. 11 It is worth more than several points of discount, because it converts a bet on one generation into a bet on one vendor.

Technology refresh rights. Can you migrate to the next generation mid-term, on what notice, at what price? Without this, a multi-year commitment obliges you to keep running depreciating silicon while the market moves past it. Reserving a single generation for several years buys supply certainty and sells away suitability.

Goldman Sachs believes discussions around AI capital expenditure (capex) are far from over. As large tech firms continue to compete for computing power, land, electricity, and data center resources, the supply-demand imbalance in AI infrastructure is likely to persist through the first half of 2028, meaning investors will continue to see higher capex guidance in the coming years. Eric Sheridan, head of TMT research at Goldman Sachs, noted there remains a significant gap between current AI computing power demand and available supply, with storage prices, chip costs, and data center construction expenses all rising. Pressure points across the AI industrial chain have expanded beyond a mere GPU shortage to include memory, land, electricity, data center enclosures, and delivery lead times.
